extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, public opinion, political science, and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for identifying and critiquing stereotypes, codes, and myth-making in public opinion and political argument; focuses on cognitive traps (contradiction, space, time, assumptions) that distort perception and reporting. Useful for journalists, analysts, and students assessing claims and propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect internal contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for a series of mutually inconsistent principles or blanket claims within an argument; contradictions indicate that differing stereotypes are being invoked to censor uncomfortable facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: "The series of contradictions showed that for each sector that stereotype was employed which would obliterate all the facts that interfered with the claim." Practical test: map the principles used to justify parts of a claim — if they blanket each other or contradict, treat the claim as suspect. Example: Ruritanian territorial claims invoking different principles (historic right, cultural superiority, natural frontier) for adjacent sectors; this rapid switching is a clue to false absolutism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for selective attention / confirmation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimant calls attention only to facts that support their stereotype and diverts or censors those that contradict it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: "When a system of stereotypes is well fixed, our attention is called to those facts which support it, and diverted from those which contradict." Anti-pattern: relying on volumes of anecdotes or statistics that only bolster a preconceived narrative while ignoring counter-evidence. Remedy: actively seek disconfirming facts and weigh them equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose underlying assumptions about facts and human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the hidden map of human nature, institutional assumptions, and historical views that a moral code or argument presupposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann argues that moral codes rest on pictures of human nature and history: "At the core of every moral code there is a picture of human nature, a map of the universe, and a version of history." Practical step: make these implicit assumptions explicit (e.g., uniform vs. varying human motives) and test whether they are warranted in the specific case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate moral judgments from empirical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing an argument, distinguish value-laden prescriptions from the factual claims on which they rest; reexamine the 'visions of the facts' rather than merely comparing ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: "Useful discussion, then, instead of comparing ideals, reexamines the visions of the facts." Anti-pattern: debating which moral code is superior without questioning the factual premises that support each code. Remedy: ask which facts are being assumed and whether different fact-visions would change moral conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess emotional loading and prejudice in stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect whether a stereotype is 'loaded with preference, suffused with affection or dislike' and whether sentiment is masquerading as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: "The stereotypes are loaded with preference, suffused with affection or dislike..." Indicator: vivid labels (e.g., 'dangerous Red', 'lazy Hindu') and strong affective language. Countermeasure: strip emotive language and re-evaluate the underlying factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative perceptions rather than attributing bad faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Before concluding an opponent is dishonest or perverse, consider that they may be seeing a different set of facts shaped by different stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: "The last explanation that we ever look for is that he sees a different set of facts." Practice: ask how the same incident would appear from another code or vantage point; this can reveal perceptual differences rather than moral failings and reduce unproductive demonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test spatial plausibility (account for space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether an argument properly accounts for geographical distance, logistics, and practical geography rather than relying on an abstract or schematic spatial image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: supporters demanded a recreated 'Eastern Front' as if Japan could be projected to Poland — "they had projected that army ... on a magic carpet." Checklists: measure actual distances, transport routes, capacities, and bottlenecks; beware of reasoning that treats maps or schematic lines as if they captured operational realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess practical geography and transportation constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Go beyond geometric distance to consider available transportation, schedules, capacities, costs, and terrain when evaluating spatial claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: "In practical life space is a matter of available transportation, not of geometrical planes... I must know that it is nine miles for a motor car, and also, if that is the case, that six of them are ruts and puddles." Practical test: identify the means of movement (ships, roads, rails), their condition and availability, and incorporate these into any feasibility assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess temporal perspective and appropriate time-conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the argument applies the correct time frame (immediate, short-term, long-term, constitutional) to the problem; misuse of time-scales distorts judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: "An important part of wisdom is the ability to distinguish the time-conception that properly belongs to the thing in hand." Examples of error: treating a short emergency as a permanent condition (or vice versa), attempting to fix indefinite future conduct (excessively detailed wills or rigid constitutions). Remedy: clarify the relevant horizon (hours, years, generations) and test claims against that horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of simplified models becoming myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for theoretical or schematic models (economic diagrams, archetypes) being popularized into 'economic mythology' and then read back into reality as literal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: economists' simplified diagram "was retailed and popularized until for large sections of the population it prevailed as the economic mythology of the day." Anti-pattern: using an abstract model's idealized agents or conditions to explain complex real-world outcomes without checking fit. Remedy: identify model assumptions and compare them with on-the-ground facts before accepting model-driven explanations.
